questions.text: Quick Revision - Heredity and Mendel's Experiments

definitionBean.title: Heredity and Mendel's Laws
definitionBean.definition: The transmission of traits from parents to offspring is called 'Heredity'; Gregor John Mendel is known as the father of genetics who conducted his experiments on pea plants[cite: 11].
definitionBean.explanation: Based on his hybridization experiments (Monohybrid and Dihybrid Cross), Mendel propounded the Law of Dominance, Law of Segregation, and Law of Independent Assortment[cite: 11].
importantPoints: Heredity: Transmission of traits from generation to generation[cite: 11]
Mendel's experiment: Selection of pea plant (Pisum sativum)[cite: 11]
Dominant trait: Those which express themselves in the first generation[cite: 11]
Recessive trait: Those which remain hidden and may appear later in offspring[cite: 11]

questions.text: Quick Revision - Sex Determination and Evolution

definitionBean.title: Sex Determination and Evolution
definitionBean.definition: Whether a newborn in humans is a boy or a girl depends on its sex chromosomes; and the emergence of new species through gradual changes in organisms is called 'Evolution'[cite: 11].
definitionBean.explanation: Humans have 23 pairs of chromosomes, out of which 22 pairs are autosomes and 1 pair is sex chromosomes (XX in females and XY in males). The father's X or Y chromosome determines the sex of the child[cite: 11].
importantPoints: Female sex chromosomes: XX, Male sex chromosomes: XY[cite: 11]
Homologous Organs: Same structure, different functions[cite: 11]
Analogous Organs: Different structure, same functions[cite: 11]

parts.statement: What is heredity? Why did Mendel select a pea plant for his experiment?
parts.correct_answer: Transmission of parental traits to offspring is heredity[cite: 11].
parts.explanation: The process of transfer of parental traits to offspring is called heredity[cite: 11]. Mendel selected the pea plant because its plants were easily available, had a short lifespan, possessed distinct contrasting traits (tall-dwarf, yellow-green), and both self-pollination and cross-pollination could be easily carried out[cite: 11].

parts.statement: What is the difference between dominant and recessive traits? Give an example[cite: 11].
parts.correct_answer: Dominant traits appear in the F1 generation, recessive ones do not[cite: 11].
parts.explanation: Traits that clearly appear in the first generation (F1) of hybridization are called dominant traits (e.g., tallness); and traits that remain hidden are called recessive traits (e.g., dwarfism)[cite: 11].

parts.statement: How is the sex of a child determined in humans? Give a diagram or explanation[cite: 11].
parts.correct_answer: Father's X or Y chromosome determines sex[cite: 11].
parts.explanation: In humans, females have XX and males have XY chromosomes[cite: 11]. The egg from the mother always carries an X chromosome, while the sperm from the father can carry either an X or a Y chromosome[cite: 11]. If the father's X chromosome combines, it results in a girl, and if a Y chromosome combines, it results in a boy[cite: 11]. Thus, the father's chromosome is primarily responsible for determining the sex of the child[cite: 11].

parts.statement: Explain homologous and analogous organs with examples[cite: 11].
parts.correct_answer: Homologous: same structure, different function; Analogous: different structure, same function[cite: 11].
parts.explanation: Homologous organs are those that have a common fundamental structure and embryonic origin but perform different functions (e.g., forelimbs of a frog, bird, and human); analogous organs are those that have different anatomical structures but perform similar functions (e.g., wings of a bird and wings of a bat)[cite: 11].
